title: Why the ocean is salty
desc: The ocean is salty because rivers and rocks slowly add dissolved minerals, including salt, and when water evaporates, most of that salt stays behind. It isn't as simple as someone pouring a shaker into the sea. Different parts of the ocean can be a little more or less salty, and freshwater lakes work differently because they have other ways to lose water and minerals.

title: Why ice floats
desc: Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water. As water freezes, its molecules form a more open structure, so the same mass takes up more space. That's unusual compared with many substances, and it matters in nature because ice can sit on top of a lake instead of sinking and freezing the whole body of water from the bottom.

title: Hibernation
desc: Hibernation is a long, deep rest some animals use in cold seasons, with a slower body and less need for food. Not every animal that sleeps a lot in winter is a true hibernator, and different species do it in different ways. It's a survival strategy, not laziness. Bears are a commonly mentioned example, though biologists sometimes debate how their sleep compares with smaller hibernators.

title: Animal migration
desc: Migration is a regular, often seasonal movement of animals from one region to another, usually for food, weather, or breeding. Birds, some fish, and some insects are well-known examples. It can cover a short distance or a huge one, and people and habitat changes can make a route harder. A map of a species' route is more useful than a single 'they all go south' line.

title: Adaptation
desc: An adaptation is a trait that helps a living thing survive and reproduce in its environment, such as a bird's beak shape or a plant that holds water. Adaptations build up in a population over many generations; one animal doesn't 'decide' to grow a new feature in a week. A trait that helps in one place might not help in another.

title: The carbon cycle
desc: The carbon cycle is the way carbon moves among the air, living things, soil, and oceans. Plants take in carbon dioxide, animals eat plants, and carbon returns to the air when living things breathe, decay, or when fuels are burned. It's a set of paths, not one circle you can memorize as a single arrow. Human burning of fossil fuels adds extra carbon to the air.

title: The Milky Way
desc: The Milky Way is the galaxy we live in: a huge system of stars, gas, and dust, including our Sun. On a dark night you can see its band as a cloudy streak of many distant stars. It isn't a path of spilled milk, and we don't see the whole shape from Earth the way a picture of another spiral galaxy looks, because we are inside it.

title: Comets versus asteroids
desc: Asteroids are rocky or metallic bodies, many of them in a belt between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are icy bodies that can grow a glowing coma and tail when they get close enough to the Sun. Both orbit in the solar system, and both are different from stars. A meteor is the flash we see when a bit of space rock burns in Earth's air.

title: Natural selection
desc: Natural selection is the idea that individuals with traits better suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so those traits can become more common over generations. It isn't a plan or a person choosing, and it doesn't mean every change is an improvement in every situation. Variation and inheritance have to be part of the picture. It's a core idea in biology class.

natural selection isn't a person choosing

title: Why bees matter
desc: Bees matter because many of them pollinate flowers, including a lot of the plants that become food. Not every bee lives in a big hive, and not all insects that look like bees are bees. Habitat, pesticides, and disease can put pressure on bee populations. You can help in small ways, like leaving some flowering plants, without needing to panic or become an expert overnight.

title: Biodiversity
desc: Biodiversity is the variety of living things in a place, from genes to species to whole ecosystems. A more diverse system can often handle change better, though it's not a simple score. People affect biodiversity through habitat, climate, and what they introduce or remove. You can think of it as more than a species count: connections matter too.

diversity of life in a place

title: How mountains form
desc: Many mountains form when Earth's plates push together and the crust folds or lifts, or when volcanoes build cones, or when a fault lifts a block of crust. Water and ice then wear them down. A mountain range can take a very long time to build. The Rockies, the Himalayas, and volcanic peaks don't all have the exact same story, but they share those big ideas.

title: The Middle Ages
desc: The Middle Ages, or medieval period, is a long stretch of European history usually placed between the end of the Western Roman Empire and the start of the early modern era. Life wasn't only knights and castles: most people farmed, and other parts of the world had their own histories at the same time. Dates are a convenience, not a switch that flipped in one year.

title: The French Revolution
desc: The French Revolution, beginning in 1789, was a period when France's monarchy was overthrown and the country went through deep, often violent political change, with ideas about rights, citizenship, and power still discussed today. It wasn't a single event. Causes included money troubles, inequality, and new political ideas. A class timeline helps more than one slogan.

title: The Enlightenment
desc: The Enlightenment was an intellectual movement, especially in the 1600s and 1700s, that emphasized reason, observation, and debate about government, rights, and knowledge. Thinkers didn't all agree, and not everyone in society gained power at once. Some of those ideas later showed up in documents and revolutions, including in the United States. A class usually names a few people and a few core claims.

title: The printing press
desc: The printing press, developed in Europe in the 1400s by Johannes Gutenberg in a well-known form, made it possible to copy books much faster than by hand. That helped ideas, news, and religious texts spread more widely, though literacy still took time to grow. Printing existed in other forms in other places too; the European press is the usual classroom focus for later European history.

title: The thirteen colonies
desc: The thirteen colonies were British colonies on the Atlantic coast of North America that later became the first U.S. states. They were not all the same: economies, religions, and relations with Native nations differed by region. They existed under British rule before the American Revolution. A map and a regional split, such as New England, the middle colonies, and the South, is the usual class view.

title: Reconstruction
desc: Reconstruction was the period after the U.S. Civil War when the country tried to reunite and to define freedom and rights for formerly enslaved people. There were real gains, then a violent backlash, and many of those gains were rolled back for a long time. It's not only a story of laws on paper. A class usually covers amendments, political conflict, and the end of that era.

title: Women's suffrage
desc: Women's suffrage is the right of women to vote. In the United States, the 19th Amendment in 1920 barred denying the vote on the basis of sex, after a long campaign, but in practice not every woman could vote equally right away because of racism and other barriers. Other countries have their own dates. A class usually covers the movement, not only one year.

desc: The Berlin Wall was a barrier built in 1961 by East Germany that divided Berlin during the Cold War, meant to stop people from leaving for the West. It stood until 1989, when it was opened and later torn down, a symbol of the Cold War's end in Europe. Families and a city were split for decades. A map of East and West Berlin helps the story make sense.

title: The United Nations
desc: The United Nations, or UN, is an international organization founded in 1945 after World War II, where member countries discuss peace, development, and other shared problems. It can pass resolutions and run programs, but it doesn't replace a country's government. It isn't a world government. A class usually covers the founding and a few of its bodies, such as the General Assembly.

title: Westward expansion
desc: Westward expansion is the 19th-century movement of the United States' claims and settlers across the continent. It is often told as a pioneer story, but it also involved the displacement, broken treaties, and violence faced by Native nations who already lived on that land, and it included forced migrations such as the Trail of Tears. title: Adding fractions
desc: To add fractions, give them a common denominator, add the numerators, and simplify if you can. For 1/4 + 1/2, rewrite 1/2 as 2/4, then add to get 3/4. Mixed numbers can be turned into improper fractions first, or you can add whole numbers and fractions separately with care. Same denominator means you only add the top numbers, not the bottoms.

title: Multiplying fractions
desc: To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators together and the denominators together, then simplify. For 2/3 × 1/4, you get 2/12, which simplifies to 1/6. You can cancel common factors first if that helps. Multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes a number smaller, which surprises people who only think of multiplication as making things bigger.

title: Dividing fractions
desc: To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal: flip the second fraction, then multiply. For 1/2 ÷ 1/4, flip 1/4 to 4/1, then multiply to get 2. A common phrase is 'keep, change, flip,' meaning keep the first fraction, change division to multiplication, and flip the second. Check with a simple picture, like how many quarter-pieces fit into a half.

title: Fractions, decimals, and percents
desc: Fractions, decimals, and percents can name the same amount in different forms. 1/2 is 0.5, which is 50 percent. To convert, you use place value and the idea that percent means per 100. Pick the form that makes the problem easier, and double-check by converting back. A simple table of common ones, like 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, is worth knowing.

title: The coordinate plane
desc: The coordinate plane is a grid with a horizontal x-axis and a vertical y-axis that meet at the origin (0, 0). A point is named (x, y): first the left-right value, then the up-down value.
